source_refs.note: Practice short questions written from Chapter 23 (PDF 101-117, printed 98-114); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 23 (Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is a carbonyl group? Name the two classes of compounds that contain it.
blocks.explanation: The structural unit >C=O is known as the carbonyl group. Aldehydes (RCHO) and ketones (RCOR') are the classes of compounds that contain a carbonyl group.

book_ref.quote: the structural unit >C=O is known as carbonyl group

blocks.prompt: 2 Where are aldehydes found in nature, and where are ketones used? Give one example.
blocks.explanation: Aldehydes are present in many spices, fruits and natural fragrances (e.g. benzaldehyde gives the smell and taste of bitter almond). Ketones are used in pharmaceuticals, chemicals and paint industries; the most common ketone, acetone, is found in nail polish removers.

book_ref.quote: Ketones used in pharmaceuticals, chemicals, and paint industries.

blocks.prompt: 3 Why is ethanal distilled off as soon as it is formed during the oxidation of ethanol?
blocks.explanation: If ethanal stays in the mixture with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ it is oxidised further to ethanoic acid. Distilling it off as soon as it forms prevents this further oxidation.

book_ref.quote: This prevents the further oxidation of ethanal to ethanoic acids.

blocks.prompt: 4 At what temperature is the mixture kept during the preparation of ethanal, and why?
blocks.explanation: Above the boiling point of ethanal (acetaldehyde) but below that of ethanol. Ethanol has the higher boiling point, so ethanal distils off while unreacted ethanol stays in the flask; pure ethanal is obtained by redistillation.

book_ref.quote: since ethanol has higher boiling point than that of acetaldehyde

blocks.prompt: 5 Why is a ketone not distilled off immediately when it is prepared from a secondary alcohol?
blocks.explanation: Under these conditions ketones are not converted into carboxylic acids, so there is no risk of further oxidation and the ketone need not be removed at once.

book_ref.quote: therefore ketone is not distilled off immediately

blocks.prompt: 6 What is formalin? Give one use.
blocks.explanation: Methanal (formaldehyde), HCHO, is a gas at room temperature; its 40 % aqueous solution is called formalin. It has a sharp, pungent smell and is used for preserving biological specimens.

book_ref.quote: HCHO is methanal (formaldehyde), not methanol (CH₃OH).

blocks.prompt: 7 How is propanone prepared from propan-2-ol? Write the equation.
blocks.explanation:
By oxidation of the secondary alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ on heating:
CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₃ + [O] → CH₃–CO–CH₃ + H₂O

book_ref.quote: Ketones are prepared by the oxidation of secondary alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 8 Differentiate between the preparation of aldehydes and ketones from alcohols.
blocks.explanation: Both are made by oxidising an alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (or KMnO₄); they differ as shown:

book_ref.quote: Aldehydes are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols

rows: Distilled off as soon as formed
Would be oxidised further to a carboxylic acid
Not converted into a carboxylic acid under these conditions

blocks.prompt: 9 Name the two basic types of reactions of carbonyl compounds.
blocks.explanation: The >C=O group governs the chemistry of aldehydes and ketones. Their two basic reactions are: (1) nucleophilic addition reactions, (2) alpha (α) carbon specific reactions.

book_ref.quote: There are two basic reactions of carbonyl compounds.

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe the hybridization and bonding of the carbonyl group.
blocks.explanation: In >C=O both carbon and oxygen are sp² hybridized. Carbon is bonded to oxygen through a double bond (one σ and one π) and to two other groups through single bonds; the group is planar.

book_ref.quote: Carbon is bonded to an oxygen atom through a double bond

blocks.prompt: 11 Why is the carbonyl group polar? Which atom is attacked by a nucleophile?
blocks.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so oxygen gets a partial negative charge (δ⁻) and carbon a partial positive charge (δ⁺). The δ⁺ carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and is attacked by nucleophiles.

book_ref.quote: Carbonyl group is polar in nature because oxygen, being more electronegative

blocks.prompt: 12 Give two reasons why the carbonyl group readily undergoes addition reactions.
blocks.explanation: (1) The π bond of C=O is easily broken, so the double bond can undergo addition. (2) The planar shape of the group makes the carbonyl carbon uncrowded, which further supports addition reactions.

book_ref.quote: planar shape of the group makes the carbonyl carbon uncrowded

blocks.prompt: 13 Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones towards nucleophiles?
blocks.explanation: (1) In a ketone the electron releasing (inductive) effect of two alkyl groups reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so it is less easily attacked. (2) The two alkyl groups get in the way of the attacking nucleophile (steric hindrance).

book_ref.quote: the electron releasing (inductive) effect of two alkyl groups reduces the positive charge

blocks.prompt: 14 What is steric hindrance? How does it affect the reactivity of ketones?
blocks.explanation: Steric hindrance is the blocking of an attacking group by bulky groups around the reaction centre. The two alkyl groups of a ketone get in the way of attacking nucleophiles, so ketones are less reactive than aldehydes.

book_ref.quote: This is also called steric hindrance.

blocks.prompt: 15 Give the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCOCH₂CH₃ and state the rule used.
blocks.explanation: 2-Methylpentan-3-one. By the rule of lowest numbers, the chain is numbered from the end nearer the C=O and the branch, so the methyl group is on C-2 (not C-4).

book_ref.quote: the chain is numbered from the end nearer the C=O and the branch

blocks.prompt: 16 How is HCN provided for its addition to carbonyl compounds, and why is it not used directly?
blocks.explanation: HCN is an extremely poisonous gas, so it is not used directly. It is produced in the mixture by slowly adding a mineral acid (HCl) to an aqueous solution of NaCN or KCN containing the carbonyl compound.

book_ref.quote: Instead, it is produced by adding slowly a mineral acid (HCl) to a mixture

blocks.prompt: 17 Why is a slight excess of KCN used in the addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound?
blocks.explanation: HCN is neither a nucleophile (no lone pair on its carbon) nor a strong acid, so it gives too few CN⁻ ions. A slight excess of KCN supplies free CN⁻ ions that start the reaction and catalyse it to a reasonable rate.

book_ref.quote: These free ions start the reaction and catalyse it to move at a reasonable rate.

blocks.prompt: 18 Write the reaction of propanone with HCN and name the product. Give its use.
blocks.explanation:
CH₃COCH₃ + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN
The product is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, a cyanohydrin; it is used as an intermediate in the manufacture of Perspex.

book_ref.quote: Propanone and HCN give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile

blocks.prompt: 19 Cyanohydrin formation is reversible. Why is the yield still high?
blocks.explanation: Both steps of cyanohydrin formation are reversible, but the equilibria lie far to the right, so most carbonyl compounds give high yields of cyanohydrins at equilibrium.

book_ref.quote: the equilibria lie far to the right

blocks.prompt: 20 What is formed when 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (from ethanal and HCN) is hydrolysed with dilute acid?
blocks.explanation:
Nitriles are hydrolysed by dilute acid to carboxylic acids, so the –CN group becomes –COOH:
CH₃CH(OH)CN → CH₃CH(OH)COOH (2-hydroxypropanoic acid)

book_ref.quote: to form carboxylic acids or carboxylate ions

blocks.prompt: 21 What are the products of reduction of propanal and of butanone with NaBH₄?
blocks.explanation:
Aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols:
CH₃CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (propan-1-ol)
CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (butan-2-ol)

book_ref.quote: With a reducing agent such as NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄

blocks.prompt: 22 What does [H] represent in the equations for reduction by NaBH₄?
blocks.explanation: [H] is the reducing hydrogen that comes from NaBH₄, written in brackets to balance the equation. It does not represent atomic hydrogen; the actual attacking species is the hydride ion, H⁻.

book_ref.quote: It does not represent atomic hydrogen.

blocks.prompt: 23 Why is the reaction of carbonyl compounds with 2,4-DNPH called an addition-elimination (condensation) reaction?
blocks.explanation: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine first adds across the C=O group and then a molecule of water is eliminated, joining the two molecules (C=N–). Adding and then losing a small molecule makes it an addition-elimination (condensation) reaction.

book_ref.quote: Aldehydes or ketones undergo a condensation reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine

blocks.prompt: 24 How is 2,4-DNPH used to identify aldehydes and ketones? Which carbonyl-containing classes do not respond?
blocks.explanation: Aldehydes and ketones give orange crystalline 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones with well-defined melting points (e.g. ethanal gives orange ethanal 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone). Carboxylic acids, esters, acyl halides and amides, though they contain >C=O, do not give this test.

book_ref.quote: This reagent is used to identify carbonyl compounds.

blocks.prompt: 25 Why are aldehydes easily oxidised while ketones are not?
blocks.explanation: To oxidise a ketone a C–C bond has to be broken, so ketones are oxidised only by strong oxidising agents. Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids by both weak and strong oxidising agents.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, ketones are only oxidized by strong oxidizing agents

blocks.prompt: 26 What is Tollens' reagent? Write the equation for its preparation.
blocks.explanation:
Tollens' reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate solution, containing silver ions in aqueous alkaline solution:
AgNO₃ + 3NH₄OH → [Ag(NH₃)₂]OH + NH₄NO₃ + 2H₂O

book_ref.quote: contains silver ions in aqueous alkaline solution

blocks.prompt: 27 How is the silver mirror formed in Tollens' test? Give its practical use.
blocks.explanation: On gentle warming with an aldehyde the silver ions are reduced to silver metal, which deposits as a silver mirror on the wall of the test tube. A dilute solution of glucose (an aldehydic sugar) was used this way to make mirrors for domestic use.

book_ref.quote: was used to make mirrors for domestic use by means of this reaction

blocks.prompt: 28 What is Fehling's solution? What happens when it is warmed with an aldehyde?
blocks.explanation:
Fehling's solution is a bright blue solution of Cu²⁺ ions in aqueous alkaline medium, complexed with a salt of tartaric acid. Warmed with an aldehyde, Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu⁺, which forms a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide:
R–CHO + 2Cu(OH)₂ + NaOH → R–COO⁻Na⁺ + Cu₂O + 3H₂O

book_ref.quote: complexed with salt of tartaric acid

blocks.prompt: 29 Distinguish between ethanal and propanone by Tollens' and Fehling's tests.
blocks.explanation: Ethanal (an aldehyde) is easily oxidised; propanone (a ketone) is not oxidised by these weak oxidising agents:

book_ref.quote: Only aldehydes give a positive Tollens' test

rows: Fehling's solution: brick-red ppt of Cu₂O
Not oxidised by weak oxidising agents

blocks.prompt: 30 Which carbonyl compounds give the iodoform test? Name the group responsible.
blocks.explanation: Only those with the CH₃CO– group, known as the acetyl (ethanoyl) group: among aldehydes only ethanal, and among ketones only methyl ketones (e.g. propanone, butanone). With I₂ and NaOH they give yellow crystalline iodoform, CHI₃.

book_ref.quote: Among aldehydes, only ethanal and among ketones, only methyl ketones possess the group CH₃CO-

blocks.prompt: 31 Write the balanced equation for the iodoform reaction of propanone.
blocks.explanation:
CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + 3NaI + 3H₂O
The yellow precipitate is iodoform; the salt formed is sodium ethanoate (sodium methanoate comes from ethanal).

book_ref.quote: CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + 3NaI + 3H₂O

blocks.prompt: 32 Why does ethanol give the iodoform test but methanol does not?
blocks.explanation:
Ethanol has the CH₃–CH(OH)– group; iodine in alkali first oxidises it to ethanal, CH₃CHO, which has the CH₃–C=O group and gives iodoform:
CH₃CH₂OH + 4I₂ + 6NaOH → CHI₃ + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H₂O
Methanol cannot give a compound with a CH₃–C=O group, so no iodoform forms.

book_ref.quote: Methanol cannot give a compound with a CH₃–C=O group, so it gives no iodoform.

blocks.prompt: 33 How many moles of I₂ and NaOH react with 0.20 mol of ethanal in the iodoform reaction?
blocks.explanation:
CH₃CHO + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃ + HCOO⁻Na⁺ + 3NaI + 3H₂O
I₂ = 0.20 × 3 = 0.60 mol; NaOH = 0.20 × 4 = 0.80 mol (and 0.20 mol CHI₃ forms).

book_ref.quote: These compounds react with iodine in the presence of sodium hydroxide

blocks.prompt: 34 Give the common names and natural sources of three carboxylic acids.
blocks.explanation: Methanoic acid (formic acid) – found in ants; ethanoic acid (acetic acid) – found in vinegar; butanoic acid (butyric acid) – in rancid butter.

book_ref.quote: Common examples of carboxylic acids are methanoic acid

blocks.prompt: 35 Why do lower carboxylic acids have high boiling points?
blocks.explanation: Their molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another (two acetic acid molecules even join as a hydrogen-bonded dimer). Extra energy is needed to break these bonds, so lower acids are liquids with high boiling points (ethanoic acid b.p. 118 °C).

book_ref.quote: Lower carboxylic acids are generally liquids at room temperature, having high boiling points.

blocks.prompt: 36 What is glacial acetic acid? Why does ethanoic acid solidify in winter?
blocks.explanation: The melting point of ethanoic acid is 17 °C, close to room temperature (25 °C), so it solidifies in winter. The solid form of pure ethanoic acid is called glacial acetic acid because it resembles glaciers.

book_ref.quote: this is why it solidifies in winter

blocks.prompt: 37 What are fatty acids? Why are they insoluble in water?
blocks.explanation: Long chain aliphatic monocarboxylic acids are called fatty acids, e.g. stearic, palmitic and oleic acids, found in vegetable oils as triglycerides. They are insoluble in water due to their long hydrophobic alkyl chains.

book_ref.quote: Stearic acid, palmitic acid, and oleic acid are found in vegetable oils

blocks.prompt: 38 Compare the solubility in water of ethanoic acid and stearic acid.
blocks.explanation: Both have the –COOH group, but they differ as follows:

book_ref.quote: Due to their ability to form the hydrogen bond, lower acids

blocks.prompt: 39 How is propanoic acid prepared from propan-1-ol? Give the conditions.
blocks.explanation:
Propan-1-ol is refluxed with excess acidified KMnO₄ or acidified K₂Cr₂O₇; it is oxidised first to propanal and then to propanoic acid:
CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O

book_ref.quote: The starting material is refluxed with excess of either acidified KMnO₄ or acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.

blocks.prompt: 40 In the oxidation of ethanol, how do the conditions decide whether ethanal or ethanoic acid is obtained?
blocks.explanation: Product is decided by the conditions:

book_ref.quote: Oxidation of ethanol and ethanal to ethanoic acid

rows: Oxidant added drop wise to warm ethanol
Product distilled off as soon as formed
Oxidation goes on to the acid

blocks.prompt: 41 How is ethanoic acid obtained from ethanenitrile by alkaline hydrolysis?
blocks.explanation:
In alkali the nitrile first gives the salt of the acid; acidification then gives the free acid:
CH₃CN + NaOH + H₂O → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + NH₃
CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl

book_ref.quote: which yield carboxylic acids on acidification

blocks.prompt: 42 Compare the acid and alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate.
blocks.explanation: Both are carried out by refluxing the ester:

book_ref.quote: the ester is hydrolyzed to carboxylic acid or carboxylate ion

rows: Goes to completion (acid becomes its salt)
Acidify the salt to get ethanoic acid

blocks.prompt: 43 How is benzoic acid prepared from methylbenzene?
blocks.explanation:
Methylbenzene (toluene) is readily oxidised by acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇; the –CH₃ side chain becomes –COOH:
C₆H₅CH₃ + 3[O] → C₆H₅COOH + H₂O

book_ref.quote: Methyl benzene is readily oxidized by acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇ to benzoic acid.

blocks.prompt: 44 Name the three types of reactions of carboxylic acids.
blocks.explanation: (1) Reactions involving the acidic hydrogen only (with metals, alkalis, carbonates). (2) Reactions involving replacement of the –OH group (SOCl₂, PCl₅, esterification). (3) Reactions involving the carboxyl group as a whole (e.g. reduction by LiAlH₄).

book_ref.quote: Reactions involving the acidic hydrogen only.

blocks.prompt: 45 Write equations for the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium metal and with sodium carbonate.
blocks.explanation:
2CH₃COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + H₂
2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O
Both occur because the acid gives H⁺ ions.

book_ref.quote: Carboxylic acids show considerable acidic character because they give H⁺ ions in water.

blocks.prompt: 46 Which gas, and how many moles of it, are given by 0.30 mol of ethanoic acid with excess NaHCO₃?
blocks.explanation:
CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O
Ratio 1 : 1, so 0.30 mol of CO₂ gas is evolved (effervescence).

book_ref.quote: The balanced equation is CH₃–COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃–COO⁻Na⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O.

blocks.prompt: 47 Compare the reactions of ethanoic acid with SOCl₂ and with PCl₅.
blocks.explanation: In both, the –OH group of the acid is replaced by Cl to give ethanoyl chloride:

book_ref.quote: in which the OH group is replaced by some other group like X, OR, NH₂ etc.

blocks.prompt: 48 Write the esterification of methanoic acid with ethanol and name the ester.
blocks.explanation:
Heated with concentrated H₂SO₄:
HCOOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ HCOOC₂H₅ + H₂O
The ester is ethyl methanoate.

book_ref.quote: Reaction with alcohols (Esterification)

blocks.prompt: 49 Which reducing agent reduces ethanoic acid to ethanol? Name two that cannot.
blocks.explanation:
The powerful reducing agent lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH₄:
CH₃COOH + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O
H₂/Ni and sodium tetrahydridoborate(III), NaBH₄, will not reduce carboxylic acids.

book_ref.quote: Other common reducing agents H₂/Ni and sodium tetrahydridoborate (III) will not reduce carboxylic acids.

blocks.prompt: 50 Define reduction in terms of hydrogen, oxygen, electrons and oxidation state.
blocks.explanation: Reduction is: gain of H₂ (or H⁻), loss of O or O₂, loss of X₂ (halogens), gain of electrons, and decrease in oxidation state. Oxidation is the opposite of each.

book_ref.quote: iv. Gain of electrons v. Decrease in Ox state.

blocks.prompt: 51 Which structural feature makes methanoic acid a reducing agent? How is it identified?
blocks.explanation: Methanoic acid, H–COOH, has an aldehydic portion (H–C=O) as well as a carboxylic portion. It is oxidised by weak and strong oxidising agents, so it gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and a brick-red ppt with Fehling's solution – the only monocarboxylic acid to do so.

book_ref.quote: The aldehydic and carboxylic portions of methanoic acid

blocks.prompt: 52 Write the reaction of methanoic acid with Fehling's solution.
blocks.explanation:
H–COOH + 2Cu(OH)₂ → Cu₂O + CO₂ + 3H₂O
Cu₂O is the brick-red precipitate; methanoic acid is oxidised to CO₂ and water.

book_ref.quote: brick red precipitates with Fehling's solution

blocks.prompt: 53 Give the oxidation numbers of Mn and C before and after the reaction of ethanedioic acid with acidified KMnO₄.
blocks.explanation:
2KMnO₄ + 3H₂SO₄ + 5HOOC–COOH → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O
Mn: +7 (KMnO₄) → +2 (MnSO₄), reduced. C: +3 (ethanedioic acid) → +4 (CO₂), oxidised.

book_ref.quote: The oxidation of ethanedioic acid with acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇

blocks.prompt: 54 Arrange RCOOH, ArOH, H₂O and ROH in order of acid strength using their pKa values.
blocks.explanation: From Table 23.1: RCOOH (pKa 5) > ArOH (pKa 10) > HOH (pKa 14) > R–OH (pKa 16). Lower pKa means a stronger acid.

book_ref.quote: phenols are even more acidic than alcohols

blocks.prompt: 55 Define pKa. Calculate the pKa of an acid with Ka = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵.
blocks.explanation:
pKa = –log Ka; the lower the pKa, the stronger the acid.
pKa = –log(2.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 5 – log 2.5 = 5 – 0.40 = 4.60

book_ref.quote: Higher the Ka or lower the pKa, stronger will be the acid and vice versa.

blocks.prompt: 56 How does delocalisation make the ethanoate ion stable?
blocks.explanation: In ethanoate, CH₃COO⁻, the negative charge is delocalised over the carbon and both oxygen atoms of –COO⁻, so its intensity on any one oxygen decreases. The stabilised ion is less likely to accept H⁺ and re-form the undissociated acid, so ethanoic acid ionises.

book_ref.quote: Due to this, the ethanoate ion becomes stabilized

blocks.prompt: 57 Differentiate between the effects of +I and –I groups on the acidity of carboxylic acids.
blocks.explanation: The group attached to –COOH changes the stability of the carboxylate ion:

book_ref.quote: The presence of an electron donating group (+I effect)

blocks.prompt: 58 Why is methanoic acid stronger than ethanoic acid?
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen is the reference for inductive effects and has no –I effect. In ethanoic acid the CH₃ group has a +I effect, which intensifies the negative charge on ethanoate and destabilises it. So methanoic acid is about 10 times stronger.

book_ref.quote: methanoic acid is 10 times stronger acid than ethanoic acid

blocks.prompt: 59 Calculate the Ka of chloroethanoic acid (pKa 2.86) and of ethanoic acid (pKa 4.74). Which is stronger?
blocks.explanation:
Ka = 10^–pKa
Chloroethanoic acid: 10^–2.86 = 1.4 × 10⁻³
Ethanoic acid: 10^–4.74 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵
Chloroethanoic acid has the larger Ka (about 76 times), so it is stronger, because Cl (–I) stabilises the anion.

book_ref.quote: indicating that it is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.74)

blocks.prompt: 60 Why is trichloroethanoic acid comparable in strength to some mineral acids?
blocks.explanation: It has three electronegative Cl atoms, each with a –I effect, which together strongly disperse the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilise it. Its pKa falls to 0.64 (ethanoic acid 4.74), comparable to some mineral acids.

book_ref.quote: Trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃C-COOH) has a pKa of 0.64

blocks.prompt: 61 What are esters? Give two uses.
blocks.explanation: Esters are derivatives of carboxylic acids obtained by their reactions with alcohols, e.g. ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₂H₅. Uses: as solvents, and as flavouring agents in fruit drinks and sweets (the fragrance and taste of fruits are due to esters).

book_ref.quote: Esters are the derivatives of carboxylic acids that are obtained by their reactions with alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 62 Why is the boiling point of ethyl ethanoate (77 °C) lower than that of ethanoic acid (118 °C)?
blocks.explanation: Unlike carboxylic acids and alcohols, esters cannot form hydrogen bonds among their molecules, so less energy is needed to separate them. Hence ethyl ethanoate boils lower and is more volatile.

book_ref.quote: This is why their boiling points are lower than the corresponding alcohols and carboxylic acids.

blocks.prompt: 63 Compare ethyl ethanoate with ethanoic acid in hydrogen bonding, boiling point and solubility.
blocks.explanation: They differ because only the acid forms hydrogen bonds:

book_ref.quote: A lower boiling point means a higher volatility.

blocks.prompt: 64 What is Fischer's esterification? Give one example.
blocks.explanation:
The reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in acidic medium to form an ester and water is Fischer's esterification. It is an equilibrium. Example:
CH₃CH₂COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOC₂H₅ (ethyl propanoate) + H₂O

book_ref.quote: This reaction is known as Fischer's esterification.

blocks.prompt: 65 Differentiate between preparing an ester from a carboxylic acid and from an acyl chloride.
blocks.explanation: Both react with an alcohol to give an ester:

book_ref.quote: Acyl chlorides react vigorously with alcohols to form esters

blocks.prompt: 66 Write the hydrolysis of ethyl benzoate.
blocks.explanation:
Aromatic esters are hydrolysed (acid- or base-catalysed) like aliphatic esters, giving an aryl carboxylic acid and an alcohol:
C₆H₅COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → C₆H₅COOH + C₂H₅OH

book_ref.quote: Aromatic esters are also hydrolysed in the same manner

blocks.prompt: 67 What are acyl chlorides? Give their general formula and name CH₃COCl.
blocks.explanation: Acyl chlorides have the functional group –COCl; saturated aliphatic ones have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COCl. In IUPAC they are named alkanoyl halides: CH₃COCl is ethanoyl chloride.

book_ref.quote: Saturated aliphatic acyl chlorides have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COCl.

blocks.prompt: 68 Why are acyl chlorides used to prepare other functional derivatives of carboxylic acids?
blocks.explanation: Acyl chlorides are the most reactive of the functional derivatives of carboxylic acids, so they react readily (e.g. with alcohols and phenol to give esters, with water to give acids) and are prepared for making other derivatives.

book_ref.quote: they are usually prepared in such a way that they can be used for the preparation of other functional derivatives

blocks.text: 23.9 Hydrolysis of Acyl Chlorides, Alkyl Chlorides and Aryl Chlorides

blocks.prompt: 69 Why is ethanoyl chloride hydrolysed within a few minutes?
blocks.explanation:
Its carbonyl carbon is attached to two highly electronegative atoms, O and Cl, whose strong electron withdrawing effect gives it a large δ⁺. The nucleophilic attack of H₂O is therefore very fast:
CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl

book_ref.quote: due to the strong electron withdrawing effect of two highly electronegative atoms

blocks.prompt: 70 Why does chlorobenzene not undergo hydrolysis like chloroethane?
blocks.explanation: In chlorobenzene the C–Cl carbon is part of the benzene ring. A lone pair on chlorine takes part in delocalisation with the π electrons of the ring, giving the C–Cl bond double bond character. The bond becomes so strong that it does not break.

book_ref.quote: lone pair on chlorine participates in delocalization

blocks.prompt: 71 Differentiate between ethanoyl chloride and chloroethane in the ease of hydrolysis.
blocks.explanation: Both are attacked by water as a nucleophile at a δ⁺ carbon:

book_ref.quote: In ethyl chloride, the carbon gets comparatively less partial positive charge

rows: Carbon attached to O and Cl
